title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
extended_summary:
This paper reviews a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, focusing on how scaffolding has been conceptualized, what forms it takes in classroom practice, and whether it is effective. The authors note that the term scaffolding has been used inconsistently across educational research, often as a broad synonym for support, and they aim to clarify the construct by synthesizing the literature.

The review analyzes 66 English-language SSCI-listed articles published between 1998 and 2009 in primary and secondary education. The paper distinguishes three key characteristics of scaffolding: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility. It also proposes a framework separating scaffolding means (feeding back, hints, instructing, explaining, modeling, questioning) from scaffolding intentions (direction maintenance, cognitive structuring, reduction of degrees of freedom, recruitment, and contingency management/frustration control). Most included studies were descriptive and concentrated on literacy, though math and science studies were also present.

Across the reviewed studies, scaffolding was most often examined in face-to-face classroom interactions, sometimes in one-to-one tutoring and sometimes in whole-class or small-group settings. The review concludes that scaffolding appears effective in the limited body of experimental and quasi-experimental research, especially for metacognitive and cognitive outcomes, but that the field is hindered by measurement problems and the lack of a shared operationalization. The authors call for better instruments, stronger fidelity checks, and more research in naturalistic classroom settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review of scaffolding research, not an empirical evaluation of a specific intervention. It synthesizes prior studies but does not itself use a controlled or observational design to estimate effects.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact estimate is reported in this paper, and it does not evaluate a technology or intervention relevant to the requested ChatGPT-in-middle-school-math topic. The article is useful conceptually for scaffolding, but it provides no measurable impact for this taxonomy.
